metadata.title: Qualcomm vs. Arm Holdings Q4 2026 trial: royalties and contract breach

content.text:
Qualcomm and Arm Holdings returned to federal court in Delaware on Monday, with Qualcomm alleging that Arm refused to hand over chip testing tools owed under their contract and disclosed a termination threat to the press in a way that hurt Qualcomm's business dealings, according to Reuters.
In the lawsuit, Qualcomm is seeking to stop paying royalties to Arm for up to five years — a remedy potentially worth billions of dollars — though Judge Maryellen Noreika is weighing whether to strike that term, which would limit the damages Qualcomm could pursue, according to Reuters.
Qualcomm, one of Arm's largest customers, further claims that Arm's disclosure of the 2024 termination threat to journalists undermined ongoing chip deal negotiations with Meta Platforms, according to Reuters. Arm, which is owned by Japan's SoftBank Group, has rejected the breach-of-contract allegations and characterized any claimed harm to Qualcomm's chip deals as too speculative to stand. Arm has also argued that Qualcomm should be barred from recovering damages related to the leak, pointing out that Qualcomm itself disclosed confidential information about antitrust investigations involving Arm to reporters, according to Reuters.
The five-day jury trial opens a new chapter in an increasingly contentious relationship between the two companies. Running concurrently is a separate bench trial in which Judge Noreika will consider whether Arm fulfilled its duty to bargain in good faith during negotiations over the next generation of its chip architecture. That licensing agreement between the two companies remains in effect until 2033, according to the outlet.
Arm disclosed the litigation in its most recent quarterly filing, noting that Qualcomm filed the original complaint in April 2024, then amended it twice in 2025 and again in March 2026 to add additional breach-of-contract claims, including an allegation that Arm failed to negotiate certain license terms in good faith.
Qualcomm described the case in its own quarterly filing, saying its complaint seeks an order compelling Arm to fulfill its contractual obligations, damages, and other relief. Qualcomm said it has not recorded any accrual for potential losses from the matter, as it does not consider a loss probable at this time.
The companies have been entangled in litigation since 2022, when Arm sued Qualcomm alleging breach of a license agreement tied to Qualcomm's acquisition of chip startup Nuvia. A jury in December 2024 found in Qualcomm's favor on the central claims in that case, and a federal court upheld that verdict in September 2025. Arm has appealed that ruling to the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.
Arm, long a behind-the-scenes supplier of chip design technology to companies including Qualcomm and Nvidia, has moved in recent years to enter the chip market itself, turning former customers into rivals, according to the outlet.
